newsitem.title: THAILAND: WEEK AHEAD - Weak bias seen for Thai stocks, baht.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Weak bias seen for Thai stocks, baht.

text.p: The Thai baht and the local stock market are likely to stay under pressure this week in the face of lingering political unease and continuing currency turmoil in Asia, analysts said on Sunday.
Worries surrounding the Thai baht may overshadow the positive sentiment generated by a rescue loan package from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Asian nations for Thailand, analysts said.
The IMF is expected to formally approve the package, which last week was estimated at $16 billion, on August 21.

"The baht's decline has been halted temporarily by the IMF-initiated rescue loan pledge, but it may come under renewed pressure due to the ongoing Asian currency turmoil," said Masaya Motono, a manager at Sakura Bank Ltd in Singapore.
"Then the baht could fall through 32.00 to the dollar or even test its historic low of 32.70 in the very near-term."
The baht stood at 31.75/31.85 per dollar on the onshore market late on Friday, compared with 31.50/31.60 late on Thursday. The offshore rate was quoted at 31.70/31.80.

A sharp drop in the Dow in New York on Friday and unrelenting pressure on other Asian stock and currency markets was expected to add to the pessimistic mood, although the Thai market has been concerned solely with domestic issues for the last couple of months.
Stock market sentiment is also expected to be dampened by a slew of poor corporate earnings last week reflecting the country's economic downturn, analysts said.
Slumping quarterly profits in telecom and property sectors dragged the benchmark SET Index down 5.44 points to end at 623.25 on Friday.

In order to improve the sagging image of the government, Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh reshuffled his cabinet on Friday to bring in a veteran economist and a business tycoon turned politician, but the move failed to impress the market.

Simmering public discontent has heightened the chances of major political upheaval and is a further setback to stock investors, who are looking for political stability at least until the IMF loan package is approved, analysts said.
Public anger has mounted against harsh government economic measures such as a hike in value added tax to 10 percent from seven percent on Saturday.

The Thai cabinet is due to consider the details of a proposed budget cut of between $1.6 billion to $2.3 billion at its weekly meeting on Tuesday. The drawing up of a new constitution is also due to be debated by parliament from September 3.
Of further concern is the baht's longer term outlook, with analysts predicting a further softening to 33 or even 35 to the dollar towards the year's end.

"The most positive thing (for the baht) is the fact that the IMF is there and the most negative thing is that other Asian currencies are going down," George Morgan, country chief executive of ABN Amro Hoare, said.
The IMF's presence should lend the baht some support, but regional currency turmoil could mean the baht would sink to 33 or even 35 to the dollar, he said.
Purchasing power parity suggests the baht should be around 30, but such a level would not be approached anytime soon, he said.

"I wouldn't expect much appreciation in another 12 months or so...it is not likely to have any strong rebound until the economy is on the mend," he added. -- Bangkok newsroom (662)-6520642 -- email:bangkok.newsroom@reuters.com
